content: Your doctor has prescribed antihemophilic factor (human) to help your blood clot effectively. This medication will be administered either by direct injection into your vein or through an intravenous (IV) fluid that drips into your vein over 5 to 10 minutes. The frequency of administration will depend on your doctor’s assessment, and it may be given as often as every other day. Antihemophilic factor (human) is a naturally occurring substance in your body that activates clotting factors in your blood to reduce bleeding episodes. In some cases, this medication may be used for other purposes, so consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Your healthcare provider will monitor the effectiveness and potential side effects of your treatment through laboratory tests and physical exams. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how well your symptoms respond to the medication. Before starting antihemophilic factor (human), inform your doctor and pharmacist if you have ever had an allergic reaction to this medication or any other drugs. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are currently taking, especially aminocaproic acid (Amicar), anticoagulants like warfarin (Coumadin), corticosteroids such as prednisone, cyclophosphamide (Cytoxan), cyclosporine (Neoral, Sandimmune), heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin (Lovenox, Normiflo), interferon alfa (Roferon-A, Intron), vincristine (Oncovin), vitamin K, and other vitamins. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor. If you become pregnant while on this medication, contact your doctor immediately. If you are scheduled for surgery, including dental procedures, inform your doctor or dentist that you are taking antihemophilic factor (human). Be aware that this medication is derived from human plasma, which carries a small risk of containing viruses such as HIV or hepatitis. Discuss these risks with your doctor. Before administering antihemophilic factor (human), inspect the solution carefully. It should be clear and free of any floating particles. Check the bag or container for leaks by gently squeezing it. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Instead, use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. Follow your healthcare provider’s instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not stop your treatment or alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you encounter a mechanical issue, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may advise you to stop the infusion. If this happens, contact your healthcare provider immediately to resume your therapy. Antihemophilic factor (human) may cause side effects. Notify your healthcare provider if you experience any of the following minor side effects, especially if they persist or worsen: dizziness, headache, sore throat, itching, upset stomach, vomiting, or tiredness. However, if you experience severe side effects, such as an increased pulse rate, hives, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, chest discomfort or tightness, chills, or fever, stop the infusion immediately and contact your healthcare provider. Serious side effects should also be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Your healthcare provider will likely supply you with several doses of antihemophilic factor (human) at a time and provide instructions on how to prepare each dose. Keep your supplies in a clean, dry place and out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will also instruct you on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving antihemophilic factor (human) through a vein or under the skin, be aware of the signs of a catheter-related infection. Notify your healthcare provider immediately if you notice tenderness, warmth, irritation, drainage, redness, swelling, or pain near the catheter site. This medication is available under several brand names, including Alphanate®, Hemofil® M, Humate-P®, Koate®-DVI, Monarc-M®, and Monoclate-P®. It is also known by other names such as AHF, AHG, and Factor VIII.
